1596.title: Compliance Module

1597.body: An OP Stack chain must be able to condition every deposit and withdrawal that crosses its canonical bridge. The OptimismPortal stores one optional hook address. While that address is address(0), the chain behaves exactly as any default OP Stack chain. When it is set, the Portal offers every item (see Item ) to the hook before any value reaches its recipient. For each item, the hook can answer in one of three ways: Proceed. The item executes as it would on any default OP Stack chain. Hold. The item is deferred. The protocol takes custody of its value and commits to running it later, unchanged. Reject. The call reverts and the item is refused while nothing is consumed. See Screening Outcome for the mechanics of each answer. The hook is an interface, so any contract can implement it. These pages specify the interface, one reference implementation called the ComplianceModule, and the interface between that module and the policy owned by the chain, which decides what is acceptable. What a policy decides is outside this specification. The feature is specified across four further pages: OptimismPortal . The hook address, the IBridgeHook interface, how the Portal names an item, commits to its terms, and runs a held item later. L1StandardBridge . How the escrow of a held token transfer moves to the hook and back. Policy . The IPolicy interface, and what a hook requires of any policy behind it. ComplianceModule . The reference hook implementation, which owns the verdict registry, custody of held value, and completion.
1597.title: Overview

1598.body: Some chains must condition value crossing their canonical bridge, and must enforce that condition where it cannot be bypassed. Screening at the sequencer only covers transactions submitted to it. It does not cover deposits submitted to L1, which carry forced inclusion, so the sequencer has no say in whether they are included. Withdrawals finalize on L1, outside the sequencer's reach. Since both deposits and withdrawals cross the OptimismPortal, that is where the chain can enforce a screening condition that cannot be bypassed. Since the condition and the rules under which an item can pass through L1 and L2 boundaries belong to the chain, the protocol only supplies: a way to defer an item, take custody of its value, and resume it later on the terms it was deferred with.
1598.title: Problem Statement

1599.body: Every deposit and withdrawal that crosses the canonical bridge is screened through the hook, whatever it carries, except deposits sent by the ProxyAdmin owner. A zero-value deposit still executes an arbitrary L2 call chosen by an L1 sender, such as a transfer between L2 accounts. An item the hook defers has its value taken into the hook's custody, out of the protocol contracts, before any of it reaches the recipient. An item can be deferred and resumed later on identical terms , with no user action in between. An item is identified unambiguously. The condition can be switched off for new items without releasing items already held. No policy may redirect value or alter an item's terms.
1599.title: Goals

16.body: Sequencers fill the role of the block producer on an OP Stack chain. Chains may have a single Sequencer or may choose to utilize some consensus protocol that coordinates multiple Sequencers. The OP Stack currently officially only supports a single active Sequencer at any given time. In general, specifications may use the term "the Sequencer" as a stand-in for either a single Sequencer or a consensus protocol of multiple Sequencers. The Sequencer: Accepts transactions directly from Users. Observes "deposit" transactions generated on Ethereum. Consolidates both transaction streams into ordered L2 blocks. Submits information to L1 that is sufficient to fully reproduce those L2 blocks. Provides real-time access to pending L2 blocks that have not yet been confirmed on L1. The Sequencer serves an important role for the operation of an L2 chain but is not a trusted actor. The Sequencer is generally responsible for improving the user experience by ordering transactions much more quickly and cheaply than would currently be possible if users were to submit all transactions directly to L1.
16.title: Sequencers

160.body: The Channel Bank stage is responsible for managing buffering from the channel bank that was written to by the L1 retrieval stage. A step in the channel bank stage tries to read data from channels that are "ready". Channels are currently fully buffered until read or dropped, streaming channels may be supported in a future version of the ChannelBank. To bound resource usage, the Channel Bank prunes based on channel size, and times out old channels. Channels are recorded in FIFO order in a structure called the channel queue . A channel is added to the channel queue the first time a frame belonging to the channel is seen. Pruning After successfully inserting a new frame, the ChannelBank is pruned: channels are dropped in FIFO order, until total_size <= MAX_CHANNEL_BANK_SIZE, where: total_size is the sum of the sizes of each channel, which is the sum of all buffered frame data of the channel, with an additional frame-overhead of 200 bytes per frame. MAX_CHANNEL_BANK_SIZE is a protocol constant defined in the Protocol Parameters table . Timeouts The L1 origin that the channel was opened in is tracked with the channel as channel.open_l1_block, and determines the maximum span of L1 blocks that the channel data is retained for, before being pruned. A channel is timed out if: current_l1_block.number > channel.open_l1_block.number + CHANNEL_TIMEOUT, where: current_l1_block is the L1 origin that the stage is currently traversing. CHANNEL_TIMEOUT is a rollup-configurable, expressed in number of L1 blocks. New frames for timed-out channels are dropped instead of buffered. Reading Upon reading, while the first opened channel is timed-out, remove it from the channel-bank. Prior to the Canyon network upgrade, once the first opened channel, if any, is not timed-out and is ready, then it is read and removed from the channel-bank. After the Canyon network upgrade, the entire channel bank is scanned in FIFO order (by open time) & the first ready (i.e. not timed-out) channel will be returned. The canyon behavior will activate when frames from a L1 block whose timestamp is greater than or equal to the canyon time first enter the channel queue. A channel is ready if: The channel is closed The channel has a contiguous sequence of frames until the closing frame If no channel is ready, the next frame is read and ingested into the channel bank. Loading frames When a channel ID referenced by a frame is not already present in the Channel Bank, a new channel is opened, tagged with the current L1 block, and appended to the channel-queue. Frame insertion conditions: New frames matching timed-out channels that have not yet been pruned from the channel-bank are dropped. Duplicate frames (by frame number) for frames that have not been pruned from the channel-bank are dropped. Duplicate closes (new frame is_last == 1, but the channel has already seen a closing frame and has not yet been pruned from the channel-bank) are dropped. If a frame is closing (is_last == 1) any existing higher-numbered frames are removed from the channel. Note that while this allows channel IDs to be reused once they have been pruned from the channel-bank, it is recommended that batcher implementations use unique channel IDs.
160.breadcrumbs: OP Stack Protocol » Clients » Rollup Node » Derivation » Channel Bank
160.title: Channel Bank

1600.body: Support for the L1ERC721Bridge or third-party bridge contracts. Transactions users submit to the sequencer. The type of policy applied by the chain governor, and the offchain service behind it.
1600.title: Non-goals

1601.body: The OptimismPortal is the screening boundary. It is the only contract that asks the hook, and it asks once per item. A deposit is screened when it is submitted while a withdrawal is screened when it is finalized. A deposit that already emitted TransactionDeposited is on its way to L2. A withdrawal whose call the Portal forwarded has already run. Neither can be recalled. graph LR U[User] OP[OptimismPortal] SB[L1StandardBridge] CM["ComplianceModule (the hook, holds value)"] POL["Policy (chain-specific)"] subgraph onchain [On chain] OP SB CM POL end U -->|deposit / finalize| OP U -->|token deposit| SB SB <-->|"messages, through the messenger"| OP OP -->|"hold / restore escrow"| SB OP <-->|"screen / hold / complete"| CM CM <-->|"screenDeposit / screenWithdrawal / screenRelease"| POL POL -->|recordVerdict| CM The OptimismPortal stores the hook address and calls the hook from depositTransaction and finalizeWithdrawalTransaction when one is set. It recognizes the messages the two canonical bridges exchange, and it commits the terms of every item it defers. The L1StandardBridge gains two entry points, callable only by the Portal, that move the escrow of a token transfer to the hook and back. It keeps its own accounting and reads its own messages. The ComplianceModule implements the hook. It owns the verdict registry, custody of any held value, and completion. It also decodes canonical messages to name the real parties for the policy. It is the only new contract that holds value. The policy decides what items go through based on its own set of rules. The Portal gains the ability to defer an item and resume it later, which a rate limiter, a per-token pause or a circuit breaker would use the same way. Each contract moves only the value it holds. A hold is the Portal's own record, and the bridge keeps none. The Portal recognizes the messenger envelope and hands the bridge the message inside it. The bridge decodes that inner call itself, moves the escrow it names, and updates its own accounting. The Portal builds every item and records its terms, and the hook only picks which item moves. No policy, however it is written, can redirect value or change what an item does. It can delay an item or refuse it, and nothing else. Letting the L1StandardBridge screen its own token transfers looks simpler, because the parties arrive there as typed arguments. It does not work for withdrawals. A token withdrawal reaches the bridge inside the messenger's relay, after the Portal has already consumed the withdrawal. A revert there becomes a failed message rather than a rejection, so the bridge could hold an item but never refuse one.
1601.title: Architecture

1603.body: An Item is one deposit or one withdrawal, as the OptimismPortal sees it. It can carry ETH, tokens, or no value at all. The Portal builds an item from the sender, target, value and call it sees. Each item is unique in its direction.
1603.title: Item

1604.body: An Identifier is an item's name, a hash of all of the item's fields. The OptimismPortal and the hook compute it the same way, so both agree on which item a Verdict names, and the verdict covers every term. The identifier is built the same way for both directions: the Portal fills the same Item fields and hashes them. The direction field keeps a deposit and a withdrawal apart, and the nonce field holds the withdrawal's nonce or, for a deposit, the Deposit Counter . Take two deposits from the same address for the same amount, to the same L2 address in the same L1 block. Every field except nonce is identical, so without the Deposit Counter both would share one identifier, and a clearance for one would release the other.
1604.title: Identifier

1605.body: Screening is offering an item to the hook, which answers with a Screening Outcome . A deposit is screened when it is submitted. A withdrawal is screened when it is finalized.
1605.title: Screening

1606.body: A Screening Outcome is the hook's answer for one item. There are three possible outcomes: Proceed. The item takes the normal path, unchanged. Hold. The item is deferred. The Portal commits its terms and its value moves to the hook. Reject. The call reverts and nothing is consumed. A rejected deposit never happens, and a rejected withdrawal remains finalizable and can be attempted again. A hook need not use all three. An asynchronous policy proceeds or holds and never rejects. A synchronous policy proceeds or rejects and never holds. See Item Lifecycle for how an item moves between them.
1606.title: Screening Outcome

1607.body: The Hook is the contract at the OptimismPortal's hook address. The Portal asks it about every item and the hook takes custody of held value. Any contract that implements IBridgeHook can be a hook.
1607.title: Hook

1608.body: A Terms Commitment is the OptimismPortal's record of a held item. It is keyed by the item's Identifier in both directions, so it binds every term. Only an item that matches a commitment can complete , and only once.
1608.title: Terms Commitment

1609.body: A Verdict is a decision about one item, recorded through the Policy against the item's Identifier . A verdict can be recorded before the item exists. It carries an expiry set by the Verdict Writer when it is written, and the policy can revoke it earlier. A clear verdict is what lets value move. With one, a withdrawal pays out at finalization and a held item can complete, as long as the policy still allows it when the value moves. An item without one is uncleared.
1609.title: Verdict

161.body: In this stage, we decompress the channel we pull from the last stage, and then parse batches from the decompressed byte stream. See Channel Format and Batch Format for decompression and decoding specification.
161.breadcrumbs: OP Stack Protocol » Clients » Rollup Node » Derivation » Channel Reader (Batch Decoding)
161.title: Channel Reader (Batch Decoding)

1610.body: Completion is moving a held item to its original destination, on the committed terms. Anyone can start it at the hook once the item has been cleared. A held item cannot be partially completed, and it is never returned to its sender.
1610.title: Completion

1611.body: A Policy is a contract the chain owns that decides the Screening Outcome for an item. The hook asks it when an item is screened and when value moves, and takes verdicts only from it.
1611.title: Policy

1612.body: The Parties of an item are the addresses the policy screens for it. For a message sent through the messengers, the hook decodes the real sender and recipient from the envelope. Where it stops decoding, it uses the sender and target of the last layer it read.
1612.title: Parties

1613.body: A Token Bridge Message is a token transfer between the L1StandardBridge and the L2StandardBridge, sent through the messengers. The OptimismPortal recognizes it in two steps. The item's outer sender and target must be the messengers, and the envelope must decode to a finalizeBridgeERC20 call from the standard bridge. Since nobody can choose those fields, a message that matches came from the bridge. The Portal fills the item's token fields from that inner call, and moves escrow only for such a message.
1613.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » Token Bridge Message
1613.title: Token Bridge Message

1614.body: The Finalizable Time of a withdrawal is the later of proofMaturityDelaySeconds after its proof was submitted and disputeGameFinalityDelaySeconds after that proof's dispute game resolved. The OptimismPortal requires both delays before it finalizes, so neither alone decides when a withdrawal can move. The game must also be proper, respected and resolved in the defender's favour, but those conditions carry no time and so are not part of this value. A withdrawal can be proven more than once, by different submitters and against different games, and whoever finalizes names which proof to use. The Finalizable Time belongs to that proof, not to the withdrawal. The Portal passes it to the hook at screening, so a policy can decide how long to wait before it holds an uncleared withdrawal.
1614.title: Finalizable Time

1615.body: graph LR E["item enters the Portal"] S{"hook is asked"} P["proceeds, as on a default chain"] R["reverted, nothing happened"] H["held: terms committed, custody with the hook"] V["verdict recorded"] C["completed on the original terms"] E --> S S -->|proceed| P S -->|reject| R S -->|hold| H H -.-> V V --> C An item is offered to the hook once when it enters. If it is held, it is checked again when its value moves, so the policy is consulted twice on a held item. A verdict lives against an Identifier , not against the item itself. The identifier must name exactly one item, otherwise one clearance could release another.
1615.title: Item Lifecycle

1616.body: The contract holding the value is the one that hands it to the hook. The OptimismPortal decides when. ETH moves through the Portal. Every ETH route, through the bridge or through the messenger, ends at the Portal. On a hold, the Portal sends the ETH to the hook. On completion it comes back as the value of the completion call, and the Portal checks it against the committed terms. Tokens move through the bridge. The L1StandardBridge escrows them, and it is the only contract that moves them to the hook and back. Tokens native to L2 are burned and minted rather than escrowed, so only their message is held, and the value behind such an item stays in the L2StandardBridge's escrow until it completes. For a Token Bridge Message , the Portal hands the bridge the inner message and asks it to move escrow. The bridge decodes that inner call itself, runs its own checks, and records the balance change in its own accounting. It records nothing about the hold: Hold. The Portal calls the bridge with the inner finalizeBridgeERC20 message it is holding. The bridge checks the selector, reads the tokens and the amount from it, and debits its escrow for that token pair, which reverts if the escrow is short. It then sends the tokens to the hook. Completion. The hook approves the bridge for the item's amount and calls the Portal, which asks the bridge to take the tokens back and credit its escrow. The normal path then runs, so a deposit is emitted to L2 and a withdrawal is relayed. The bridge does not depend on the hook, because only the Portal can send its escrow to the hook or take it back.
1616.title: Custody Model

1617.body: A chain that sets a hook address accepts the following, on top of the trust model of a default OP Stack chain. The chain is not a Stage 1 Rollup. A hook that holds indefinitely is a permanent Withdrawal Liveness failure caused by an actor that is neither the Security Council nor the Proxy Admin Owner. Users have to trust the chain operator not to censor them. Whoever can upgrade the hook is the custodian of all deferred value. That authority is not constrained to be the chain's ProxyAdmin owner. What an upgraded hook does with value already in its custody is outside the protocol's guarantees. The exposure is not limited to what is held at any one moment. A hostile hook holds every new deposit and withdrawal as it arrives, so its custody grows with the chain's bridge flow for as long as it stays set. It still cannot redirect value or alter an item's terms. See iCM-003 . Removing the hook strands held items. The chain's ProxyAdmin owner can remove the hook at any time. New items stop being screened, but every item already held stays held. Its commitment stays in the Portal and its value stays with the removed hook. The policy decides who can clear an item. A compromised policy can complete held items early, and so can any role it trusts. The value still only reaches the item's original destination. A compromised policy can also hold or refuse any new item. A failing policy can halt bridging. The ComplianceModule's disable switch exists so that a problem in the policy, or a long outage of the Verdict Writer, cannot block new deposits and withdrawals indefinitely. It is not a release. While it is on, every deposit proceeds without the policy being asked, and so does every withdrawal initiated at or after the cutoff. Items already held, and withdrawals initiated before the cutoff, are still screened. A problem in the hook itself is fixed by upgrading it.
1617.title: Trust Assumptions

1618.body: The change is limited to L1 contracts, with no multi-client or consensus impact. A held deposit emits no TransactionDeposited event, so the derivation pipeline sees nothing until the deposit completes, and then sees an ordinary deposit. For a chain that does not set a hook, behavior does not change, but three things change either way: The L1StandardBridge gains two entry points that only the OptimismPortal can call. The OptimismPortal gains completion functions, while existing user entry points are unchanged. The OptimismPortal makes the L1StandardBridge an Unsafe Target , so a withdrawal that calls the bridge directly can no longer be finalized. For a chain that enables it, these assumptions break: A successful depositTransaction no longer implies that the deposit reaches L2. A successful ERC-20 deposit, and the ERC20DepositInitiated and SentMessage events it emits, no longer imply that the deposit reaches L2. finalizeWithdrawalTransaction can revert for a withdrawal that is not cleared, and once the hook holds it, it can succeed without paying the recipient. Held deposits complete out of submission order, because a verdict for a later item can land first. A RelayedMessage event still implies the recipient was paid, because a withdrawal is held before the messenger relays it.
1618.title: Backward Compatibility

1619.body: No hook is set by default, so developers on chains that do not enable it see no difference. For a chain that enables it: A deposit may be held. The bridge call succeeds, no TransactionDeposited event is emitted, and the value sits with the hook. The item completes later with no further action from the user. SDKs and bridge interfaces should watch the hook's events and show a pending state rather than success. A withdrawal that is not cleared cannot be finalized until it is, and the revert lets a bridge interface show it as pending. Once the policy stops waiting, finalizing it holds it, so the recipient is not paid until completion. Integrators that bridge programmatically, including contracts that call depositTransaction directly, have to handle the held case rather than assuming the deposit succeeds atomically. Bridges and escrows outside the core contracts should treat a deposit as pending until it completes. Tooling is able to find the hook through the OptimismPortal's hook address.
1619.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » Impact on Developer Experience
1619.title: Impact on Developer Experience

162.body: During the Batch Buffering stage, we reorder batches by their timestamps. If batches are missing for some time slots and a valid batch with a higher timestamp exists, this stage also generates empty batches to fill the gaps. Batches are pushed to the next stage whenever there is one sequential batch directly following the timestamp of the current safe L2 head (the last block that can be derived from the canonical L1 chain). The parent hash of the batch must also match the hash of the current safe L2 head. Note that the presence of any gaps in the batches derived from L1 means that this stage will need to buffer for a whole sequencing window before it can generate empty batches (because the missing batch(es) could have data in the last L1 block of the window in the worst case). A batch can have 4 different forms of validity: drop: the batch is invalid, and will always be in the future, unless we reorg. It can be removed from the buffer. accept: the batch is valid and should be processed. undecided: we are lacking L1 information until we can proceed batch filtering. future: the batch may be valid, but cannot be processed yet and should be checked again later. The batches are processed in order of the inclusion on L1: if multiple batches can be accept-ed the first is applied. An implementation can defer future batches a later derivation step to reduce validation work. The batches validity is derived as follows: Definitions: batch as defined in the Batch format section . epoch = safe_l2_head.l1_origin a L1 origin coupled to the batch, with properties: number (L1 block number), hash (L1 block hash), and timestamp (L1 block timestamp). inclusion_block_number is the L1 block number when batch was first fully derived, i.e. decoded and output by the previous stage. next_timestamp = safe_l2_head.timestamp + block_time is the expected L2 timestamp the next batch should have, see block time information . next_epoch may not be known yet, but would be the L1 block after epoch if available. batch_origin is either epoch or next_epoch, depending on validation. Note that processing of a batch can be deferred until batch.timestamp <= next_timestamp, since future batches will have to be retained anyway. Rules, in validation order: batch.timestamp > next_timestamp -> future: i.e. the batch must be ready to process. batch.timestamp < next_timestamp -> drop: i.e. the batch must not be too old. batch.parent_hash != safe_l2_head.hash -> drop: i.e. the parent hash must be equal to the L2 safe head block hash. batch.epoch_num + sequence_window_size < inclusion_block_number -> drop: i.e. the batch must be included timely. batch.epoch_num < epoch.number -> drop: i.e. the batch origin is not older than that of the L2 safe head. batch.epoch_num == epoch.number: define batch_origin as epoch. batch.epoch_num == epoch.number+1: If next_epoch is not known -> undecided: i.e. a batch that changes the L1 origin cannot be processed until we have the L1 origin data. If known, then define batch_origin as next_epoch batch.epoch_num > epoch.number+1 -> drop: i.e. the L1 origin cannot change by more than one L1 block per L2 block. batch.epoch_hash != batch_origin.hash -> drop: i.e. a batch must reference a canonical L1 origin, to prevent batches from being replayed onto unexpected L1 chains. batch.timestamp < batch_origin.time -> drop: enforce the min L2 timestamp rule. batch.timestamp > batch_origin.time + max_sequencer_drift: enforce the L2 timestamp drift rule, but with exceptions to preserve above min L2 timestamp invariant: len(batch.transactions) == 0: epoch.number == batch.epoch_num: this implies the batch does not already advance the L1 origin, and must thus be checked against next_epoch. If next_epoch is not known -> undecided: without the next L1 origin we cannot yet determine if time invariant could have been kept. If batch.timestamp >= next_epoch.time -> drop: the batch could have adopted the next L1 origin without breaking the L2 time >= L1 time invariant. len(batch.transactions) > 0: -> drop: when exceeding the sequencer time drift, never allow the sequencer to include transactions. batch.transactions: drop if the batch.transactions list contains a transaction that is invalid or derived by other means exclusively: any transaction that is empty (zero length byte string) any deposited transactions (identified by the transaction type prefix byte) any transaction of a future type > 2 (note that Isthmus adds support for SetCode transactions of type 4 and Lagoon adds PostExec transactions of type 0x7d) If no batch can be accept-ed, and the stage has completed buffering of all batches that can fully be read from the L1 block at height epoch.number + sequence_window_size, and the next_epoch is available, then an empty batch can be derived with the following properties: parent_hash = safe_l2_head.hash timestamp = next_timestamp transactions is empty, i.e. no sequencer transactions. Deposited transactions may be added in the next stage. If next_timestamp < next_epoch.time: the current L1 origin is repeated, to preserve the L2 time invariant. epoch_num = epoch.number epoch_hash = epoch.hash If the batch is the first batch of the epoch, that epoch is used instead of advancing the epoch to ensure that there is at least one L2 block per epoch. epoch_num = epoch.number epoch_hash = epoch.hash Otherwise, epoch_num = next_epoch.number epoch_hash = next_epoch.hash

1621.body: This page specifies what the OptimismPortal gains when a chain enables a bridge hook. The model those changes serve, and the vocabulary they use, are in the Compliance Module overview . The Portal is the only contract that asks the hook. It builds every Item , offers it to the hook, commits the terms of every item the hook defers, and runs a deferred item later on exactly those terms. Everything the hook can do, it does through the four functions in IBridgeHook .
1621.title: Overview

1623.body: The Bridge Hook Address is network-specific state on the Portal. It is set only through initialize , by the ProxyAdmin or its owner, and cleared only by removeHook . While it is address(0), the Portal behaves as on a default OP Stack chain. The L1StandardBridge does not hold the hook address. The Portal is the contract that moves the bridge's escrow when an ERC-20 deposit or withdrawal is held. Removing the hook stops screening for new items and strands every item already held. Its commitment stays in the Portal, and its value stays with the removed hook.
1623.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Bridge Hook Address
1623.title: Bridge Hook Address

1624.body: An Unsafe Target is an address a withdrawal may not call. The default set is the OptimismPortal itself and the ETHLockbox. This page adds the L1StandardBridge on every chain, and the Bridge Hook Address while it is set. See Why the Bridge and the Hook Are Unsafe Targets .
1624.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Unsafe Target
1624.title: Unsafe Target

1625.body: The Deposit Counter is a counter the Portal assigns to a deposit when it screens it. A withdrawal carries its own nonce, unique on L2, so it is already unique, but a deposit has no unique field of its own: two identical deposits in the same block are otherwise indistinguishable. The counter is what makes a deposit's Identifier name exactly one deposit, and the identifier exists only from the moment the counter is assigned. The counter MUST be strictly increasing and MUST never be reused, including across hook changes and re-initialization.
1625.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Deposit Counter
1625.title: Deposit Counter

1626.body:
interface IBridgeHook { function screenDeposit(Item calldata item) external returns (bool pass_); function holdDeposit(Item calldata item) external payable; function screenWithdrawal(Item calldata item, uint256 finalizableAt) external returns (bool pass_); function holdWithdrawal(Item calldata item) external payable;
} screenDeposit and screenWithdrawal carry the Screening Outcome in how they return: Outcome How the hook signals it What the Portal does Proceed returns true the item takes the normal path, unchanged Hold returns false the Portal commits the item's terms and moves its value to the hook Reject reverts the whole transaction reverts and nothing is consumed screenWithdrawal also receives finalizableAt, the Finalizable Time of the proof being finalized, so a hook can reject an uncleared withdrawal until it is ready to hold it. See Withdrawals and When They Are Held . The Portal builds its own items and commits to their terms itself. It asks the hook only what to do with them.
1626.title: IBridgeHook

1627.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Item Construction
1627.title: Item Construction

1628.body: The Portal recognizes one shape: a message between the two canonical bridges. For a deposit, the envelope's sender is the messenger, which the Portal derives from its own caller, and the messenger stamps the L1StandardBridge as the inner sender. For a withdrawal, the proven sender is the L2 messenger and the inner sender is the L2StandardBridge. In both, the inner call is finalizeBridgeERC20, and the inner target is the other canonical bridge: the L2StandardBridge for a deposit and the L1StandardBridge for a withdrawal. Nobody can choose the senders, so a message that matches came from the bridge, addressing its counterpart. The Portal marks such an item as a token transfer, and moves escrow only for it. The bridge trusts the Portal on the envelope: who sent the message, through which messenger, to which bridge. It never sees the envelope itself, only the inner finalizeBridgeERC20 call, which it decodes on its own. The recognition still has to be correct, because the bridge acts on it. It gives the Portal no new authority: the messenger already accepts relays only from the Portal, with a sender the Portal supplies, so a faulty Portal can already reach the bridge's escrow.
1628.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Routing and Recognition
1628.title: Routing and Recognition

1629.body:
mapping(bytes32 => bool) public heldDeposits; // keyed by the item's identifier
mapping(bytes32 => bool) public heldWithdrawals; // keyed by the item's identifier One bit per deferred item, recording the exact terms the protocol agreed to defer, already validated on the way in. When the hook asks to complete an item, the Portal rebuilds the key from the arguments it receives and requires the matching bit. The bridge keeps no commitments. It moves escrow only when the Portal calls, and only for a message the Portal has committed to.

1629.title: Terms Commitment

163.body: In the Payload Attributes Derivation stage, we convert the batches we get from the previous stage into instances of the PayloadAttributes structure. Such a structure encodes the transactions that need to figure into a block, as well as other block inputs (timestamp, fee recipient, etc). Payload attributes derivation is detailed in the section Deriving Payload Attributes section below. This stage maintains its own copy of the system configuration , independent of the L1 retrieval stage. The system configuration is updated with L1 log events whenever the L1 epoch referenced by the batch input changes.
163.breadcrumbs: OP Stack Protocol » Clients » Rollup Node » Derivation » Payload Attributes Derivation
163.title: Payload Attributes Derivation

1630.body: A withdrawal is screened each time someone tries to finalize it. If the hook proceeds, the withdrawal pays out through the normal path. For tokens that is the messenger and the bridge, as on a default chain. If the hook rejects, the finalization reverts. The withdrawal can be finalized again later, for example once it clears. If the hook holds, the withdrawal is marked finalized and its value moves to the hook, ETH from the ETHLockbox and tokens from the bridge's escrow. The protocol cannot force a hold, because the hook can always reject instead. How long flagged value stays in protocol contracts is therefore the chain's commitment, not the protocol's. It is kept by finalizing flagged withdrawals once the policy would hold them, which is an ordinary finalization that anyone can trigger through the existing permissionless entry points.
1630.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Withdrawals and When They Are Held
1630.title: Withdrawals and When They Are Held

1631.title: Function Specification

1632.body: Initializes the Portal. It is the only way to set the Bridge Hook Address . Only the _bridgeHook parameter is new, and the rest of the behavior is unchanged. Parameters: _bridgeHook: the contract implementing IBridgeHook , or address(0) to keep the current hook. Behavior: MUST revert if the caller is not the ProxyAdmin or its owner. MUST leave bridgeHook unchanged if _bridgeHook is address(0). MUST otherwise set bridgeHook to _bridgeHook, replacing any hook already set, and emit BridgeHookSet. MUST leave heldDeposits, heldWithdrawals and the Deposit Counter unchanged.
1632.title: initialize

1633.body: Returns the Bridge Hook Address . MUST return address(0) if the chain has not configured a hook.
1633.title: bridgeHook

1634.body: Removes the Bridge Hook Address . Behavior: MUST revert if the caller is not the ProxyAdmin owner. MUST revert with OptimismPortal_InvalidBridgeHookState if bridgeHook is address(0). MUST set bridgeHook to address(0) and emit BridgeHookRemoved with the removed hook.
1634.title: removeHook

1635.body: Accepts deposits of ETH and data. Behavior must remain unchanged while bridgeHook is address(0). Behavior, when bridgeHook is not address(0): MUST perform every check it performs on a default OP Stack chain before consulting the hook. MUST take today's normal path, unchanged, without consulting the hook, when the caller is the ProxyAdmin owner. MUST assign the Deposit Counter and build the item from it before calling the hook, so the identifier the hook screens is the identifier the Portal commits to if it holds. MUST call bridgeHook.screenDeposit with that item. MUST take today's normal path, unchanged, when screenDeposit returns true. MUST revert when screenDeposit reverts. When screenDeposit returns false, it MUST hold the deposit: MUST set heldDeposits[identifier] to true before moving any value. MUST NOT emit a TransactionDeposited event. MUST NOT lock the deposit's ETH in the ETHLockbox; the ETH goes to the hook instead. MUST ask the L1StandardBridge to move its escrow for the item, if the item is identified as a Token Bridge Message by calling holdERC20 on the L1StandardBridge. MUST then move any ETH the deposit carries to the hook by calling holdDeposit with that value. MUST emit DepositHeld with the item's identifier.
1635.title: depositTransaction

1636.body: Proves a withdrawal transaction. Behavior: MUST revert if the withdrawal target is an Unsafe Target . MUST NOT consult the hook since a withdrawal is screened when it is finalized, not when it is proven. MUST otherwise behave as on a default OP Stack chain while bridgeHook is address(0).
1636.title: proveWithdrawalTransaction

1637.body: Finalizes a withdrawal using a proof submitted by another address. Behavior: MUST revert if the withdrawal target is an Unsafe Target . MUST otherwise behave as on a default OP Stack chain while bridgeHook is address(0). Behavior, when bridgeHook is not address(0): MUST perform every check it performs on a default OP Stack chain, including checkWithdrawal, before consulting the hook. MUST mark the withdrawal as finalized before calling the hook. MUST call bridgeHook.screenWithdrawal with the item and the Finalizable Time of the proof it is finalizing, before forwarding the withdrawal call to the appropriate target. MUST take the normal path, unchanged, when screenWithdrawal returns true. MUST revert, consuming nothing and leaving the withdrawal finalizable, when screenWithdrawal reverts. When screenWithdrawal returns false, it MUST hold the withdrawal: MUST set heldWithdrawals[identifier] to true before moving any value. MUST NOT forward the withdrawal call to its target. MUST NOT emit WithdrawalFinalized, so a held withdrawal is not reported as paid. MUST unlock the withdrawal's ETH from the ETHLockbox before moving it, since the Portal pays the hook from its own balance. MUST ask the L1StandardBridge to move its escrow for the item, if the item is a recognized Token Bridge Message by calling holdERC20 on the L1StandardBridge. MUST then move the withdrawal's ETH to the hook by calling holdWithdrawal with that value. MUST emit WithdrawalHeld with the item's identifier and the withdrawal hash.
1637.title: finalizeWithdrawalTransactionExternalProof

1638.body: Executes a held deposit on the terms the Portal committed to. The Bridge Hook Address calls this function when it is ready to release the deposit. Parameters: _item: the item as it was held. The Portal rebuilds its identifier from this preimage. Behavior: MUST revert if the caller is not the Bridge Hook Address . MUST revert if heldDeposits[identifier] is not true. MUST revert if the ETH sent with the call does not match the item's committed value. MUST delete heldDeposits[identifier] before moving any value. MUST ask the L1StandardBridge to take its escrow back, if the item is a recognized Token Bridge Message by calling restoreERC20 on the L1StandardBridge. MUST then lock the ETH sent with the call in the ETHLockbox, as on the normal deposit path. MUST emit a TransactionDeposited event with the committed terms, using the item's from unchanged. MUST NOT re-derive from from msg.sender, aliased or not: the caller is the hook, and the item's from already carries the aliasing applied when the deposit was submitted. MUST NOT run the resource meter again: a completion counts only against the per-block count in Resource Metering . MUST NOT revert if the system is paused, matching depositTransaction on a default OP Stack chain.
1638.title: completeDepositTransaction

1639.body: Runs a held withdrawal on the terms the Portal committed to. The Bridge Hook Address calls this function when it is ready to release the withdrawal. Parameters: _item: the item as it was held. The Portal rebuilds the item's identifier from this preimage. Behavior: MUST revert if the caller is not the Bridge Hook Address . MUST revert if the system is paused. MUST revert if the L2 Withdrawal Sender is not DEFAULT_L2_SENDER, so a completion cannot run inside another withdrawal's execution. MUST revert if heldWithdrawals[identifier] is not true. MUST revert if the ETH sent with the call does not match the item's committed value. MUST revert if the item's target is an Unsafe Target at the time of completion. MUST delete heldWithdrawals[identifier] before moving any value. MUST NOT unlock ETH from the ETHLockbox, since the withdrawal's ETH is the value sent with the call. MUST ask the L1StandardBridge to take its escrow back, if the item is a recognized Token Bridge Message by calling restoreERC20 on the L1StandardBridge. MUST set the L2 Withdrawal Sender to the item's committed sender before forwarding the call. MUST forward the call to the target with SafeCall.callWithMinGas and the item's committed gasLimit. MUST unset the L2 Withdrawal Sender after the call returns. MUST revert if the forwarded call fails, so the withdrawal stays held and can be completed again later. This diverges from finalizeWithdrawalTransaction, which records the failure as finalized with success = false. MUST emit WithdrawalFinalized with success as true.
1639.title: completeWithdrawalTransaction

164.body: In the Engine Queue stage, the previously derived PayloadAttributes structures are buffered and sent to the execution engine to be executed and converted into a proper L2 block. The stage maintains references to three L2 blocks: The finalized L2 head : everything up to and including this block can be fully derived from the finalized (i.e. canonical and forever irreversible) part of the L1 chain. The safe L2 head : everything up to and including this block can be fully derived from the currently canonical L1 chain. The unsafe L2 head : blocks between the safe and unsafe heads are unsafe blocks that have not been derived from L1. These blocks either come from sequencing (in sequencer mode) or from unsafe sync to the sequencer (in validator mode). This is also known as the "latest" head. Additionally, it buffers a short history of references to recently processed safe L2 blocks, along with references from which L1 blocks each was derived. This history does not have to be complete, but enables later L1 finality signals to be translated into L2 finality. Engine API usage To interact with the engine, the execution engine API is used, with the following JSON-RPC methods: Bedrock, Canyon, Delta: API Usage engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV2 — updates the forkchoice (i.e. the chain head) to headBlockHash if different, and instructs the engine to start building an execution payload if the payload attributes parameter is not null. engine_getPayloadV2 — retrieves a previously requested execution payload build. engine_newPayloadV2 — executes an execution payload to create a block. Ecotone: API Usage engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV3 — updates the forkchoice (i.e. the chain head) to headBlockHash if different, and instructs the engine to start building an execution payload if the payload attributes parameter is not null. engine_getPayloadV3 — retrieves a previously requested execution payload build. engine_newPayload engine_newPayloadV2 — executes a Bedrock/Canyon/Delta execution payload to create a block. engine_newPayloadV3 — executes an Ecotone execution payload to create a block. engine_newPayloadV4 - executes an Isthmus execution payload to create a block. The current version of op-node uses the v4 Engine API RPC methods as well as engine_newPayloadV3 and engine_newPayloadV2, due to engine_newPayloadV4 only supporting Isthmus execution payloads. Both engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV4 and engine_getPayloadV4 are backwards compatible with Ecotone, Bedrock, Canyon & Delta payloads. Prior versions of op-node used v3, v2 and v1 methods. The execution payload is an object of type ExecutionPayloadV3 . The ExecutionPayload has the following requirements: Bedrock The withdrawals field MUST be nil The blob gas used field MUST be nil The blob gas limit field MUST be nil Canyon, Delta The withdrawals field MUST be non-nil The withdrawals field MUST be an empty list The blob gas used field MUST be nil The blob gas limit field MUST be nil Ecotone The withdrawals field MUST be non-nil The withdrawals field MUST be an empty list The blob gas used field MUST be 0 The blob gas limit field MUST be 0 Forkchoice synchronization If there are any forkchoice updates to be applied, before additional inputs are derived or processed, then these are applied to the engine first. This synchronization may happen when: A L1 finality signal finalizes one or more L2 blocks: updating the "finalized" L2 block. A successful consolidation of unsafe L2 blocks: updating the "safe" L2 block. The first thing after a derivation pipeline reset, to ensure a consistent execution engine forkchoice state. The new forkchoice state is applied by calling fork choice updated on the engine API. On forkchoice-state validity errors the derivation pipeline must be reset to recover to consistent state. L1-consolidation: payload attributes matching If the unsafe head is ahead of the safe head, then consolidation is attempted, verifying that existing unsafe L2 chain matches the derived L2 inputs as derived from the canonical L1 data. During consolidation, we consider the oldest unsafe L2 block, i.e. the unsafe L2 block directly after the safe head. If the payload attributes match this oldest unsafe L2 block, then that block can be considered "safe" and becomes the new safe head. The following fields of the derived L2 payload attributes are checked for equality with the L2 block: Bedrock, Canyon, Delta, Ecotone Blocks parent_hash timestamp randao fee_recipient transactions_list (first length, then equality of each of the encoded transactions, including deposits) gas_limit Canyon, Delta, Ecotone Blocks withdrawals (first presence, then length, then equality of each of the encoded withdrawals) Ecotone Blocks parent_beacon_block_root If consolidation succeeds, the forkchoice change will synchronize as described in the section above. If consolidation fails, the L2 payload attributes will be processed immediately as described in the section below. The payload attributes are chosen in favor of the previous unsafe L2 block, creating an L2 chain reorg on top of the current safe block. Immediately processing the new alternative attributes enables execution engines like go-ethereum to enact the change, as linear rewinds of the tip of the chain may not be supported. L1-sync: payload attributes processing If the safe and unsafe L2 heads are identical (whether because of failed consolidation or not), we send the L2 payload attributes to the execution engine to be constructed into a proper L2 block. This L2 block will then become both the new L2 safe and unsafe head. If a payload attributes created from a batch cannot be inserted into the chain because of a validation error (i.e. there was an invalid transaction or state transition in the block) the batch should be dropped & the safe head should not be advanced. The engine queue will attempt to use the next batch for that timestamp from the batch queue. If no valid batch is found, the rollup node will create a deposit only batch which should always pass validation because deposits are always valid. Interaction with the execution engine via the execution engine API is detailed in the Communication with the Execution Engine section. The payload attributes are then processed with a sequence of: Engine: Fork choice updated with current forkchoice state of the stage, and the attributes to start block building. Non-deterministic sources, like the tx-pool, must be disabled to reconstruct the expected block. Engine: Get Payload to retrieve the payload, by the payload-ID in the result of the previous step. Engine: New Payload to import the new payload into the execution engine. Engine: Fork Choice Updated to make the new payload canonical, now with a change of both safe and unsafe fields to refer to the payload, and no payload attributes. Engine API Error handling: On RPC-type errors the payload attributes processing should be re-attempted in a future step. On payload processing errors the attributes must be dropped, and the forkchoice state must be left unchanged. Eventually the derivation pipeline will produce alternative payload attributes, with or without batches. If the payload attributes only contained deposits, then it is a critical derivation error if these are invalid. On forkchoice-state validity errors the derivation pipeline must be reset to recover to consistent state. Processing unsafe payload attributes If no forkchoice updates or L1 data remain to be processed, and if the next possible L2 block is already available through an unsafe source such as the sequencer publishing it via the p2p network, then it is optimistically processed as an "unsafe" block. This reduces later derivation work to just consolidation with L1 in the happy case, and enables the user to see the head of the L2 chain faster than the L1 may confirm the L2 batches. To process unsafe payloads, the payload must: Have a block number higher than the current safe L2 head. The safe L2 head may only be reorged out due to L1 reorgs. Have a parent blockhash that matches the current unsafe L2 head. This prevents the execution engine individually syncing a larger gap in the unsafe L2 chain. This prevents unsafe L2 blocks from reorging other previously validated L2 blocks. This check may change in the future versions to adopt e.g. the L1 snap-sync protocol. The payload is then processed with a sequence of: Bedrock/Canyon/Delta Payloads engine_newPayloadV2: process the payload. It does not become canonical yet. engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV2: make the payload the canonical unsafe L2 head, and keep the safe/finalized L2 heads. Ecotone Payloads engine_newPayloadV3: process the payload. It does not become canonical yet. engine_forkchoiceUpdatedV3: make the payload the canonical unsafe L2 head, and keep the safe/finalized L2 heads. Isthmus Payloads engine_newPayloadV4: process the payload. It does not become canonical yet. Engine API Error handling: On RPC-type errors the payload processing should be re-attempted in a future step. On payload processing errors the payload must be dropped, and not be marked as canonical. On forkchoice-state validity errors the derivation pipeline must be reset to recover to consistent state.

1640.body: A held deposit is paid for once, at submission, like any other deposit. Its gas counts against the deposit limit of the L1 block where it completes, since that is where it reaches L2. A completion that does not fit reverts and can be sent again in the next block. The resource meter is unchanged. A deposit is capped, priced and charged at submission the same way as on a default OP Stack chain, so the deposit fee still follows submissions. While a hook is set, the Portal also counts the deposit gas published in each L1 block. Ordinary deposits and completions share that count, under the same max resource limit. The count covers the whole L1 block in which a hook is set or removed. Setting a hook starts it from the gas the block already bought, and removing the hook leaves it running until the block ends. A completion is never charged again.
1640.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Resource Metering
1640.title: Resource Metering

1642.body: A protocol contract only ever executes terms it committed to. The Portal rebuilds the commitment key from the preimage it is handed at completion and requires the matching bit, so an item that does not match a commitment cannot be executed. Impact Severity: Critical If violated, a hook could run an item the protocol never agreed to defer, or run a deferred item on altered terms, redirecting value or changing what the item does on L2.
1642.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » iCM-001: A held item executes only on its committed terms
1642.title: iCM-001: A held item executes only on its committed terms

1643.body: The Portal deletes the commitment registered in either heldDeposits or heldWithdrawals before any value moves. Impact Severity: Critical If violated, a held item could be completed repeatedly, draining the Portal, the ETHLockbox or the bridge's escrow.
1643.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » iCM-002: A held item completes at most once
1643.title: iCM-002: A held item completes at most once

1644.body: The Portal builds every item and commits its terms. The hook chooses which item moves and when, never where the value goes or what the item does. Impact Severity: Critical If violated, the contract at the hook address could redirect user value or decide arbitrary execution on both L1 and L2. That is far more authority than setting a hook is meant to grant to whoever can upgrade it.
1644.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » iCM-003: A hook can only delay or refuse an item
1644.title: iCM-003: A hook can only delay or refuse an item

1645.body: While bridgeHook is address(0), every entry point behaves exactly as on a default OP Stack chain, except that the L1StandardBridge is an Unsafe Target . Impact Severity: High If violated, chains that never opted in would change behavior on upgrade, which the feature exists to avoid.
1645.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » iCM-004: A chain with no hook configured is unaffected
1645.title: iCM-004: A chain with no hook configured is unaffected

1646.body: A withdrawal carries a gas limit for the call it will make on L1. Holding splits that call into two transactions: the finalization that defers it, and the completion that executes it. The gas limit has to survive this deferring. A held withdrawal is recorded as finalized and its call does not execute. The commitment is what carries the guarantee across. completeWithdrawalTransaction forwards the call with SafeCall.callWithMinGas and the committed gasLimit, and reverts if that call fails. The target receives the gas limit the withdrawal carries, whether the withdrawal was held or not. Without this, the withdrawal is consumed at finalization, and the gas limit set on L2 would apply to nothing. Impact Severity: Critical If violated, a held withdrawal completes with less gas than its sender asked for. The target call might fail. The commitment is already deleted and cannot be retried, leaving whichever value it carries stranded.
1646.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » iCM-005: A held withdrawal keeps its minimum gas guarantee
1646.title: iCM-005: A held withdrawal keeps its minimum gas guarantee

1647.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Security Considerations
1647.title: Security Considerations

1648.body: The Portal forwards a withdrawal's call itself, so the target sees the Portal as its caller, which is the only check those entry points make. A withdrawal targeting the L1StandardBridge with a restoreERC20 call credits escrow the Portal never committed to, and one targeting the hook with a holdDeposit call writes a record for an item the Portal never held. The bridge is unsafe whether or not the chain sets a hook. Gating it on the hook would mean a withdrawal proven while bridgeHook is address(0) stops being finalizable once a hook is set. Nothing legitimate targets the bridge directly, because a token withdrawal reaches it through the L1CrossDomainMessenger. The hook is an Unsafe Target only while it is set. After removeHook or a replacement through initialize , the former hook is an ordinary target, and a withdrawal can call it with the Portal as its caller. A hook MUST therefore check that it is still the Portal's hook, with bridgeHook() == address(this), and not only that its caller is the Portal. The address can also change after a withdrawal is proven or held, so the checks can disagree. Finalization decides for a withdrawal that pays out directly, and completion decides for a held one.
1648.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Why the Bridge and the Hook Are Unsafe Targets
1648.title: Why the Bridge and the Hook Are Unsafe Targets

1649.body: Replacing or removing a hook while items are held does not move their value, which stays with the former hook. initialize is the only way to set a hook, so changing it also re-applies every other initialize argument: the SystemConfig, the AnchorStateRegistry, the ETHLockbox and the proof maturity delay. The operator must pass the current values. A wrong proof maturity delay, for example, changes when every withdrawal already proven can be finalized.
1649.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Changing the Hook
1649.title: Changing the Hook

165.body: It is possible to reset the pipeline, for instance if we detect an L1 reorg (reorganization) . This enables the rollup node to handle L1 chain reorg events. Resetting will recover the pipeline into a state that produces the same outputs as a full L2 derivation process, but starting from an existing L2 chain that is traversed back just enough to reconcile with the current L1 chain. Note that this algorithm covers several important use-cases: Initialize the pipeline without starting from 0, e.g. when the rollup node restarts with an existing engine instance. Recover the pipeline if it becomes inconsistent with the execution engine chain, e.g. when the engine syncs/changes. Recover the pipeline when the L1 chain reorganizes, e.g. a late L1 block is orphaned, or a larger attestation failure. Initialize the pipeline to derive a disputed L2 block with prior L1 and L2 history inside a fault-proof program. Handling these cases also means a node can be configured to eagerly sync L1 data with 0 confirmations, as it can undo the changes if the L1 later does recognize the data as canonical, enabling safe low-latency usage. The Engine Queue is first reset, to determine the L1 and L2 starting points to continue derivation from. After this, the other stages are reset independent of each other. Finding the sync starting point To find the starting point, there are several steps, relative to the head of the chain traversing back: Find the current L2 forkchoice state If no finalized block can be found, start at the Bedrock genesis block. If no safe block can be found, fallback to the finalized block. The unsafe block should always be available and consistent with the above (it may not be in rare engine-corruption recovery cases, this is being reviewed). Find the first L2 block with plausible L1 reference to be the new unsafe starting point, starting from previous unsafe, back to finalized and no further. Plausible iff: the L1 origin of the L2 block is known and canonical, or unknown and has a block-number ahead of L1. Find the first L2 block with an L1 reference older than the sequencing window, to be the new safe starting point, starting at the above plausible unsafe head, back to finalized and no further. If at any point the L1 origin is known but not canonical, the unsafe head is revised to parent of the current. The highest L2 block with known canonical L1 origin is remembered as highest. If at any point the L1 origin in the block is corrupt w.r.t. derivation rules, then error. Corruption includes: Inconsistent L1 origin block number or parent-hash with parent L1 origin Inconsistent L1 sequence number (always changes to 0 for a L1 origin change, or increments by 1 if not) If the L1 origin of the L2 block n is older than the L1 origin of highest by more than a sequence window, and n.sequence_number == 0, then the parent L2 block of n will be the safe starting point. The finalized L2 block persists as the finalized starting point. Find the first L2 block with an L1 reference older than the channel-timeout The L1 origin referenced by this block which we call l2base will be the base for the L2 pipeline derivation: By starting here, the stages can buffer any necessary data, while dropping incomplete derivation outputs until L1 traversal has caught up with the actual L2 safe head. While traversing back the L2 chain, an implementation may sanity-check that the starting point is never set too far back compared to the existing forkchoice state, to avoid an intensive reorg because of misconfiguration. Implementers note: step 1-4 are known as FindL2Heads. Step 5 is currently part of the Engine Queue reset. This may change to isolate the starting-point search from the bare reset logic. Resetting derivation stages L1 Traversal: start at L1 base as first block to be pulled by next stage. L1 Retrieval: empty previous data, and fetch the base L1 data, or defer the fetching work to a later pipeline step. Frame Queue: empty the queue. Channel Bank: empty the channel bank. Channel Reader: reset any batch decoding state. Batch Queue: empty the batch queue, use base as initial L1 point of reference. Payload Attributes Derivation: empty any batch/attributes state. Engine Queue: Initialize L2 forkchoice state with syncing start point state. (finalized/safe/unsafe) Initialize the L1 point of reference of the stage to base. Require a forkchoice update as first task Reset any finality data Where necessary, stages starting at base can initialize their system-config from data encoded in the l2base block. About reorgs Post-Merge Note that post- merge , the depth of reorgs will be bounded by the L1 finality delay (2 L1 beacon epochs, or approximately 13 minutes, unless more than 1/3 of the network consistently disagrees). New L1 blocks may be finalized every L1 beacon epoch (approximately 6.4 minutes), and depending on these finality-signals and batch-inclusion, the derived L2 chain will become irreversible as well. Note that this form of finalization only affects inputs, and nodes can then subjectively say the chain is irreversible, by reproducing the chain from these irreversible inputs and the set protocol rules and parameters. This is however completely unrelated to the outputs posted on L1, which require a form of proof like a fault-proof or zk-proof to finalize. Optimistic-rollup outputs like withdrawals on L1 are only labeled "finalized" after passing a week without dispute (fault proof challenge window), a name-collision with the proof-of-stake finalization.

1650.body: The hook runs before SafeCall.callWithMinGas, so finalizing a cleared withdrawal also pays for the hook. This cannot brick a withdrawal, because callWithMinGas checks the remaining gas when it makes the call, so a finalization without enough gas reverts, consumes nothing, and can be retried with more. It does cost headroom. A withdrawal whose gas limit is close to the most gas an L1 transaction can use may no longer fit in one transaction. Nothing runs inside the relay, so token withdrawals do not depend on the gas the user set on L2.
1650.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » OptimismPortal » Gas Headroom on the Withdrawal Path
1650.title: Gas Headroom on the Withdrawal Path

1651.body: A chain that has not configured a hook pays one SLOAD, which short circuits the rest of the hook logic. Proving and finalizing also read the L1StandardBridge address from SystemConfig for the unsafe-target check, which applies on every chain.

1652.title: L1StandardBridge

1653.body: This page specifies the L1StandardBridge changes to support a chain that enables a bridge hook. The model those changes serve, and the vocabulary they use, are in the Compliance Module overview . The bridge's behavior on a default OP Stack chain is specified in its contract specification . The bridge gains two entry points, callable only by the OptimismPortal, that move the escrow of a held token transfer to the hook and back. It does not store the hook address, it keeps no record of which items are held, and it never calls the hook directly. A hold is the Portal's record. The bridge is handed a message to decode and asked to move escrow for it. See Terms Commitment .
1653.title: Overview

1654.body: The bridge only receives the inner finalizeBridgeERC20 encoded call carried in a message between the L1 and L2 bridges, which it decodes on its own: it checks the selector, then reads the token pair and the amount from the call's arguments. The order of the token pair inside the message depends on the item's direction. A standard bridge encodes its message for the chain that will execute it, so the token local to the destination comes first. In a deposit's message the L1 token is therefore the second token argument, and in a withdrawal's message it is the first. The bridge is told the direction because it cannot tell the two apart from the message alone. Whether the item is a Token Bridge Message at all is the Portal's judgement, not the bridge's. The bridge trusts the Portal on the message envelope: who sent the message, through which messenger, and to which bridge. See Routing and Recognition .
1654.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » What the Bridge Receives From the Portal
1654.title: What the Bridge Receives From the Portal

1655.body: Only Native L1 Tokens are escrowed by the bridge, and only those have a deposits balance. An OptimismMintableERC20 is burned on deposit and minted on withdrawal, so there is no escrow to move for it. A held item carrying an OptimismMintableERC20 therefore moves no tokens at the bridge. Only its message is held, and the value behind it stays in the L2StandardBridge's escrow on L2 until the item completes.
1655.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » Escrowed and Minted Tokens
1655.title: Escrowed and Minted Tokens

1657.body: The OptimismPortal only asks for an escrow move for a message it has recognized as a token transfer between the two canonical bridges, and only for an item whose terms it has committed to. Mitigations Both new entry points are restricted to the OptimismPortal. The bridge stores no Portal address today, so how it resolves one is an open point. See Resolving the Portal . Both new entry points read the Portal's bridgeHook() and revert while it is address(0), so a Portal on a chain that has configured no hook cannot move escrow at all. The bridge decodes the inner call itself rather than trusting the Portal's reading of the token pair and amount. The bridge's own escrow checks still apply, so a move that would overdraw the escrow reverts. A faulty Portal can already drain the escrow through the L1CrossDomainMessenger, so these entry points add no additional capabilities to the Portal. See The Portal Could Already Reach the Escrow .
1657.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » aCM-001: The OptimismPortal is trusted
1657.title: aCM-001: The OptimismPortal is trusted

1658.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » Function Specification
1658.title: Function Specification

1659.body: Moves the escrow of a held token transfer out of the bridge and to the hook. Parameters: _direction: whether the held item is a deposit or a withdrawal. _message: the inner finalizeBridgeERC20 call the Portal is holding. Behavior: MUST revert if the caller is not the OptimismPortal. MUST revert if the Portal's bridgeHook() is address(0). MUST revert if the selector of _message is not finalizeBridgeERC20. MUST read the token pair and the amount from _message, using _direction to tell which of the two token arguments is the L1 token. MUST record whether the L1 token is a Native L1 Token , keyed by _direction and _message. MUST transfer that amount of the L1 token to the bridge hook, if the L1 token is a Native L1 Token . MUST decrease the deposits mapping for that token pair by that amount, if the L1 token is a Native L1 Token . MUST revert if the deposits balance for that token pair is below the amount. MUST NOT move any tokens if the L1 token is an OptimismMintableERC20.
1659.title: holdERC20

166.body: For every L2 block derived from L1 data, we need to build payload attributes , represented by an expanded version of the PayloadAttributesV2 object, which includes additional transactions and noTxPool fields. This process happens during the payloads-attributes queue ran by a verifier node, as well as during block-production ran by a sequencer node (the sequencer may enable the tx-pool usage if the transactions are batch-submitted).
166.breadcrumbs: OP Stack Protocol » Clients » Rollup Node » Derivation » Deriving Payload Attributes
166.title: Deriving Payload Attributes

1660.body: Takes the escrow of a held token transfer back into the bridge, so the normal path can run. Parameters: _direction: the same direction that was passed to holdERC20 . _message: the same inner finalizeBridgeERC20 call that was passed to holdERC20 . Behavior: MUST revert if the caller is not the OptimismPortal. MUST revert if the Portal's bridgeHook() is address(0). MUST revert if the selector of _message is not finalizeBridgeERC20. MUST revert if holdERC20 recorded no classification for the same _direction and _message. MUST read the token pair and the amount from _message, using _direction to tell which of the two token arguments is the L1 token. MUST pull that amount of the L1 token from the bridge hook, using the allowance the hook granted, if the recorded classification is a Native L1 Token . MUST increase the deposits mapping for that token pair by that amount, if the recorded classification is a Native L1 Token . MUST NOT move any tokens if the recorded classification is an OptimismMintableERC20. MUST clear the recorded classification. MUST NOT pay the recipient. The normal path runs after the escrow is back, so a deposit is emitted to L2 and a withdrawal is relayed, and it is the relay that pays the recipient from escrow.
1660.title: restoreERC20

1662.body: Tokens leave the bridge's escrow for the hook, and return to it, only when the OptimismPortal calls. The hook never calls the bridge, and nobody else is authorized on either entry point. Impact Severity: Critical If violated, any caller could drain the bridge's escrow to any address, taking the tokens of users whether or not they ever interacted with the hook.
1662.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » iCM-006: Bridge escrow moves only when requested by the Portal
1662.title: iCM-006: Bridge escrow moves only when requested by the Portal

1663.body: Every escrow move updates the deposits mapping for the token pair it moves, in both directions. The value of a held item is accounted for at the hook, never at the bridge. Impact Severity: Critical If violated, the bridge's accounting moves away from its real balance. Too low, and later legitimate withdrawals revert for users unrelated to the hold. Too high, and the bridge releases tokens it no longer has, which is a loss paid for by other users of the same token.
1663.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » iCM-007: The deposits balance always matches what the bridge still holds
1663.title: iCM-007: The deposits balance always matches what the bridge still holds

1664.body: Both holdERC20 and restoreERC20 take their amount from the inner finalizeBridgeERC20 call they decode. A hold and the restore that reverses it therefore move the same amount, so an item's round trip through the hook leaves the escrow where it started. Whether the L1 token is a Native L1 Token is recorded at hold and reused on restore, rather than derived again, so a token whose answer changes cannot break the round trip. Impact Severity: Critical If violated, a restore could credit more escrow than the matching hold removed, creating a balance the bridge never received. Other users of that token pair pay for it, because their withdrawals draw on the same escrow.
1664.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » iCM-008: The bridge moves exactly the amount the message names
1664.title: iCM-008: The bridge moves exactly the amount the message names

1665.body: The new entry points add no way to pay an arbitrary address. holdERC20 sends escrow to the bridge hook and nowhere else, and restoreERC20 only pulls it back from there. The recipient named in the message is paid by the relay on the normal path, once the escrow has returned. This is the bridge-side counterpart to iCM-003 . Impact Severity: Critical If violated, a hold could pay an address the item never named, which turns a mechanism for deferring value into one for redirecting it.
1665.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » iCM-009: Escrow leaves the bridge only to the hook or to the recipient
1665.title: iCM-009: Escrow leaves the bridge only to the hook or to the recipient

1666.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » Security Considerations
1666.title: Security Considerations

1667.body: The bridge's own checks still apply when the Portal asks it to move escrow. If an inner check refuses the move, the whole hold reverts, and so does the finalization that triggered it. The withdrawal stays finalizable and can be attempted again. This is the correct outcome for safety, but it is a liveness risk worth monitoring. A token whose escrow move the bridge always refuses is a token whose withdrawals can never be held, so flagged value for that token stays in the bridge's escrow indefinitely. A cleared withdrawal never needs the move, because it pays through the normal path which should remain unchanged.
1667.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » A Refused Escrow Move Refuses the Hold
1667.title: A Refused Escrow Move Refuses the Hold

1668.body: These entry points do not widen what a faulty OptimismPortal can do to the bridge. finalizeBridgeERC20 releases escrow to whoever the messenger names as the cross-domain sender. The messenger takes that name from a parameter of relayMessage. And only the Portal may call relayMessage, with an l2Sender it sets itself. A compromised portal can already drain escrow through that path on a default OP Stack chain. The existing path needs a well-formed relay through the messenger, and it leaves a RelayedMessage event and a successfulMessages entry behind. An escrow move through holdERC20 is a single call, reachable from depositTransaction, which never touched the bridge before, and it leaves no messenger record. Monitoring built on messenger events does not see it.
1668.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » The Portal Could Already Reach the Escrow
1668.title: The Portal Could Already Reach the Escrow

1669.body: Both entry points are restricted to the OptimismPortal, but the bridge has no Portal address today. Its initialize takes only the L1CrossDomainMessenger and the SystemConfig. Two existing routes could resolve one, messenger.portal() or systemConfig.optimismPortal(), and the design this page is drawn from does not choose between them. The same question applies to the destination of a held transfer. holdERC20 sends escrow to the bridge hook, and the design states that the bridge does not need the hook address, which leaves the Portal to supply it. Neither point is settled.
1669.breadcrumbs: Experimental » Compliance Module » L1StandardBridge » Resolving the Portal
1669.title: Resolving the Portal

167.body: For each L2 block to be created by the sequencer, we start from a sequencer batch matching the target L2 block number. This could potentially be an empty auto-generated batch, if the L1 chain did not include a batch for the target L2 block number. Remember that the batch includes a sequencing epoch number, an L2 timestamp, and a transaction list. This block is part of a sequencing epoch , whose number matches that of an L1 block (its L1 origin ). This L1 block is used to derive L1 attributes and (for the first L2 block in the epoch) user deposits. Therefore, a PayloadAttributesV2 object must include the following transactions: one or more deposited transactions , of two kinds: a single L1 attributes deposited transaction , derived from the L1 origin. for the first L2 block in the epoch, zero or more user-deposited transactions , derived from the receipts of the L1 origin. zero or more network upgrade automation transactions : special transactions to perform network upgrades. zero or more sequenced transactions : regular transactions signed by L2 users, included in the sequencer batch. Transactions must appear in this order in the payload attributes. The L1 attributes are read from the L1 block header, while deposits are read from the L1 block's receipts . Refer to the deposit contract specification for details on how deposits are encoded as log entries. Logs are derived from transactions following the future-proof best-effort process described in On Future Proof Transaction Log Derivation
167.breadcrumbs: OP Stack Protocol » Clients » Rollup Node » Derivation » Deriving the Transaction List
167.title: Deriving the Transaction List

1670.body: A held item carrying an OptimismMintableERC20 holds only the message. The tokens were burned on deposit, or were never minted on withdrawal, so there is nothing in the bridge for the hook to take custody of. The consequence is that such an item can only ever complete to its original recipient or stay held. Nothing, including upgrading the hook, can redirect the value, because the value is not in the hook's custody. On L2 it remains in the L2StandardBridge's escrow.
